title: karma yoga on the lecture tour
hookLine: wanted on stage, but as a costume; the tour he walked away from
carry: karma yoga: the work, never its fruits
tomorrow: he quits the tour. so where does he teach instead?

cards: Somebody asks for the accent. The outfit for the photo. The spicy-food story, again.
Being wanted, but as a costume. A poster on a town hall wall says: tonight, the Hindu monk. The hall fills.
Some people have come to learn. Some have come to see the robe and turban, the way they'd go to a traveling show.
Up front, a young man from Calcutta waits to be introduced, and he can feel the difference between the two kinds of looking.

teach.h: A TOUR THAT SOLD A NOVELTY.
teach.b: After the Parliament his name was in the papers, and his disciples' biography says a lecture bureau signed him for a tour of American towns. On paper it made sense.
He needed money, for travel and for work he hoped to start for the poor in India. But the bureau sold him as a novelty. Some audiences wanted an exotic visitor, not a teacher.
In the biography he grows uneasy, and finally breaks with the bureau, at a cost to himself, to speak on his own terms.

teach.h: KARMA YOGA: THE WORK, NOT THE FRUITS.
teach.b: The Gita names that choice: karma yoga, the yoga of action. Krishna tells Arjuna: your right is to the work, never to its fruits. And later: whatever you do, do it as an offering to me.
That's why many Hindus finish a task or a puja with a few words handing it over: Krishnarpanam astu, may it be an offering to Krishna.
Vivekananda later put it his own way in his book Karma Yoga: work like a master, not like a slave. The tour had turned him into a product with a price. Walking away turned him back into a teacher.
He kept lecturing, and now he chose the rooms. The money mattered. It just wasn't allowed to decide what his tradition looked like on an American stage.

how: Vivekananda's Karma-Yoga, drawn from his talks in America, is read by many of his followers alongside the Gita's teaching on work without clinging to its fruits.

games.q: a channel wants to film your grandmother's cooking, but only in a costume and an accent she doesn't have. what fits Vivekananda's choice?
o: take it. exposure is worth a costume.
turn it down, and offer to share the food her own way.
stop sharing her recipes outside the family.
games.why: he didn't stop teaching when the tour sold him as a novelty. he left the bureau and kept teaching on his own terms.

practice: Think of one piece of work waiting for you this week. Picture doing it well, start to finish. Then hand it over: say softly, Krishnarpanam astu, may it be an offering.
If you don't pray, say instead: the work is mine, the fruit is not. Rest your hands palms down on your knees, not reaching for anything.

wordCard.voice: Vivekananda in America: after Chicago, a paid tour that sold him as a novelty, and his choice to leave it.
